title: Normalization: one fact, one place
objectives: Spot the update, insert and delete anomalies that a fact stored in more than one place causes
Normalize a table to third normal form in working terms: one value per cell, every column about the whole key, and nothing but the key
Replace a column that can disagree with another by deriving it — in the query, a view, or a generated column (virtual by default since PostgreSQL 18)
Tell a deliberate copy (a price at the time of sale, a cached counter) from accidental duplication, and keep a cache honest
Store instants as `timestamptz` and dates as `date`, not text, and predict the rows a text comparison or an inclusive date bound silently drops

questions.prompt: `orders` stores `customer_email` on every order. Ada changes her email, and the account page updates it on her most recent order only. What has happened?

options.text: An update anomaly — customer 7 now has two emails in the database and nothing says which is current
Nothing wrong: old orders should keep the email they were placed with
An insert anomaly — the new email couldn't be stored
The update fails with a foreign-key error

questions.explanation: The email is a fact about the *customer*, stored once per *order*, so every change has to touch every copy — and this one didn't. The fix is one home for the fact (`customers.email`) and a pointer to it. The "keep the old email" option describes a *snapshot*, which would be a deliberate, documented choice; this column is read as "the customer's email", so two values for it is simply a contradiction.

questions.prompt: Course titles and room numbers are stored only on `enrollments` rows, one copy per enrolled student. Which problems does that cause? (Pick two.)

options.text: When the last student drops a course and that enrollment row is deleted, the course's title and room are gone too
A new course can't be recorded until someone enrolls in it
Deleted enrollments keep the course visible until `VACUUM` runs
A student can't enroll in more than one course

questions.explanation: Both are anomalies from storing the course's facts on a table about enrollments. The delete anomaly: removing one fact (an enrollment) destroys an unrelated one (the course). The insert anomaly: you can't store the course without inventing an enrollment. Give courses their own table and let `enrollments` hold only the link. Deleted rows aren't visible to queries after the delete commits, whatever `VACUUM` has or hasn't done; and one row per enrollment allows any number of courses per student — the problem is what else each row carries.

questions.prompt: `products.tags` is a `text` column holding values like `"red,outdoor,sale"`. Which normal form does that break, and what's the practical cost?

options.text: 1NF — the cell holds a list, so you can't put a foreign key on a tag, and `LIKE '%red%'` also matches `infrared`
2NF — `tags` depends on only part of the key
3NF — `tags` depends on a non-key column
None — a string is a single value, so the table is normalized

questions.explanation: First normal form is "one value per cell": a delimited list is a repeating group squeezed into a string. You can't constrain each tag, you can't index tag lookups cleanly, renaming a tag means string surgery on every row, and substring matching gives false hits. A `product_tags(product_id, tag_id)` join table fixes all of it. 2NF and 3NF are about which *key* a column depends on — the problem here comes earlier.

questions.prompt: `order_items` has `PRIMARY KEY (order_id, sku)` and columns `qty`, `product_name`. What's wrong with `product_name` here?

options.text: It depends on only part of the key (`sku`), so it's repeated on every order that sells that product — it belongs in `products` (2NF)
Nothing; every column depends on the primary key because the key identifies the row
It breaks 1NF because names can contain spaces
It needs its own index to be in 2NF

questions.explanation: Ask of each column: "to know this, do I need the whole key?" `qty` needs both `order_id` and `sku`. `product_name` needs only `sku`, so rename a product and you must update every line that ever sold it. 2NF only matters with a multi-column key — and the "the key identifies the row, so everything depends on it" answer is exactly the reasoning it exists to correct.

questions.prompt: `orders(id, ordered_at, customer_id, customer_city)` — `id` is the key. Which normal form does `customer_city` break?

options.text: 3NF — it depends on `customer_id`, a non-key column, not on the order itself
2NF — it depends on part of a composite key
1NF — cities are repeated
None — it's on the same row as the key, so it depends on the key

questions.explanation: Third normal form: non-key columns depend on the key *and nothing but the key*. The city is determined by the customer, so it changes when the customer moves, not when the order changes — and every order holds a copy. The key here is a single column, so 2NF can't be the problem. Move the city to `customers` (unless you mean "the city this order shipped to", which is a snapshot — a different fact).

questions.prompt: `invoices` has both `is_paid boolean` and `paid_at timestamptz`, and production has rows where they disagree. What's the most robust fix?

options.text: Keep `paid_at` and derive `is_paid` from `paid_at IS NOT NULL` (in queries, a view, or a generated column)
Keep both and add `CHECK (is_paid = (paid_at IS NOT NULL))`
Keep both, and make one service function responsible for writing them together
Keep both and run a nightly job that repairs mismatches

questions.explanation: When one column can be computed from another, storing both creates a way to be wrong. Deriving removes the second write and so removes the bug class. The `CHECK` is a decent stopgap when legacy readers need the column — it makes disagreement impossible to write — but every writer still has to set both. A service function guards only the code that calls it (not scripts or the SQL editor), and a nightly repair job means the data is wrong for up to a day, and it has to guess which column was right.

questions.prompt: You try `orders.total numeric GENERATED ALWAYS AS ((SELECT sum(quantity * unit_price) FROM order_items WHERE order_id = id))`. What happens?

options.text: It's rejected (`cannot use subquery in column generation expression`) — a generated column sees only its own row; use a view or compute it in the query
It works in PostgreSQL 18, because virtual columns are computed when read
It works if you add `STORED`
It works, but the total goes stale when `order_items` changes

questions.explanation: The manual: a generation expression can only use immutable functions and can't use subqueries or reference anything other than the current row. Virtual vs stored changes *when* it's computed, not *what it can see*. A total over child rows belongs in a view (`CREATE VIEW order_totals AS SELECT order_id, sum(…) … GROUP BY order_id`) or in the query that needs it; a same-row value like `quantity * unit_price` is the generated column's job.

questions.prompt: A reviewer says `order_items.unit_price` duplicates `products.price` and should be dropped in favour of a join. Are they right?

options.text: No — it records what this order was charged, a different fact; joining to the current price would rewrite past orders
Yes — the same value in two tables is always a normalization error
Yes, unless a trigger keeps `unit_price` in sync with `products.price`
No — but only because a join would be slower

questions.explanation: The test isn't "is the value repeated?" but "is it the same fact?" Ask: if the catalogue price changes tomorrow, should last month's invoice change? No — so `unit_price` is a snapshot, and storing it is correct. A trigger keeping it in sync would make it *wrong*: it would turn the snapshot back into a copy of today's price. Performance has nothing to do with it.

questions.prompt: `posts.comment_count` is a deliberate cache. The API inserts a comment and commits, then runs `UPDATE posts SET comment_count = $1` with a count it computed in Node. Counts drift. Which change keeps the cache honest?

options.text: Update it in the same transaction as the insert, relative to itself (`comment_count = comment_count + 1`, e.g. from an `AFTER INSERT OR DELETE` trigger), and keep a query that rebuilds it from `comments`
Keep the code and recompute every count in a nightly job
Compute the count in Node inside a mutex so two requests can't interleave
Make `comment_count` a generated column that counts the post's comments

questions.explanation: Three separate bugs drift the count: the update runs in a second transaction (if it fails, the comment exists and the count never moves), the value is computed from a read (two requests both read 5 and both write 6), and only the API maintains it (a script or the SQL editor doesn't). Same transaction + relative update + a trigger fixes all three, and the rebuild query is the recovery path. A nightly job leaves it wrong for up to a day; an in-process mutex doesn't cover other server instances or other writers; a generated column can only see its own row, so it can't count comments.

prompts.prompt: Derive `is_paid` from `paid_at` so it can never disagree with it.
code: SELECT id, amount, paid_at, paid_at ___ AS is_paid
prompts.explanation: A view stores the query, not the data, so every read computes `paid_at IS NOT NULL` from the one stored column. There's no second value to update — and nothing to drift.

prompts.prompt: A same-row derived value that you also need to index. In PostgreSQL 18, finish the definition.
prompts.explanation: `GENERATED ALWAYS AS (expr)` defines a generated column. Since PostgreSQL 18 it's virtual by default (computed on read), and PostgreSQL 18 can't index a virtual generated column — so a column you want to index needs `STORED` (computed on write). Before PostgreSQL 18, `STORED` was the only kind and was always required.

prompts.prompt: Pick column types that make the database understand the values: a due date (no time of day) and the moment a row was created.
prompts.explanation: `date` holds a calendar day with no time or zone, and rejects `2026-02-30` at insert. `timestamptz` converts any input offset to UTC and stores the instant, so comparisons are between instants rather than between strings that happen to look like dates.

prompts.prompt: All rows created from March 1 to March 10 inclusive, correct for any timestamp precision.
prompts.explanation: A half-open range: include the start, exclude the next day's start. `<= '2026-03-10'` would mean "up to midnight at the *start* of March 10" and drop that whole day, for a `timestamptz` column and (as a string prefix) for a `text` one.

code: -- created_at is TEXT holding ISO strings:
snippets.question: What count comes back?
snippets.explanation: Text compares character by character, and `'2026-03-10'` is a prefix of both March 10 timestamps, so it sorts *before* them — both fall outside `<= '2026-03-10'`. Only the March 9 row qualifies. The last day of every such report is silently missing.

code: -- due_on is TEXT holding date-only values: '2026-03-09', '2026-03-10', '2026-03-11'
snippets.question: Which rows come back?
snippets.explanation: Now the short string is in the column: `'2026-03-10'` is a prefix of `'2026-03-10T00:00:00.000Z'`, so it compares as *less*, and the tasks due on the 10th — the ones the query is for — are dropped. A `date` column compared with a date parameter has no such trap.

code: -- created_at is TIMESTAMPTZ now, same four instants:
snippets.question: What count comes back?
snippets.explanation: The type is right now, but `'2026-03-10'` as a `timestamptz` means midnight at the *start* of March 10 (in the session's time zone), so both March 10 rows are later than it. Fixing the type removes the string traps; the inclusive upper bound needs a half-open range: `>= '2026-03-01' AND < '2026-03-11'`.
